message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact download/upload speeds right now.  
But you can check it yourself in a couple of quick ways:

---

## 1. Use an online speed‑test website  
The simplest method is to visit one of the popular speed‑test sites:

| Site | URL |
|------|-----|
| Speedtest by Ookla | https://www.speedtest.net |
| Fast.com (Netflix) | https://fast.com |
| Google Speed Test | type “speed test” in Google and click the built‑in test |

Just open the page, click “Go” (or “Start”), and it will report your download, upload, and ping.

---

## 2. Run a command‑line test (Windows)

If you prefer a terminal/command‑prompt approach, you can use **speedtest‑cli**.  
It’s a lightweight Python script that reports the same metrics as the web UI.

### Step 1 – Install speedtest‑cli (if you haven’t already)

```cmd
pip install speedtest-cli
```

> *If you don’t have `pip` installed, you can get it by installing Python from https://python.org.*

### Step 2 – Run the test

```cmd
speedtest-cli --simple
```

This will output something like:

```
Ping: 12.34 ms
Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
```

---

## 3. Quick test via PowerShell (no extra install)

If you’re on Windows 10/11, you can use PowerShell’s `Invoke-WebRequest` to hit a public speed‑test endpoint:

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://www.speedtest.net/api/api.php -Method Head
```

This won’t give you bandwidth numbers, but it can confirm that you’re connected to the internet.

---

### What to do if you get no results

* **Firewall/Antivirus blocking** – Temporarily disable or allow the tool.
* **No internet** – Check your router/modem, cables, or contact your ISP.
* **Speed lower than expected** – Try restarting your modem/router, or run the test at different times of day.

---

Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the results or troubleshooting any issues!
